newsitem.title: USA: Automakers agree to step up airbag research.
newsitem.headline: Automakers agree to step up airbag research.

text.p: Following complaints that airbags are too dangerous, the U.S. Big Three automakers said Wednesday they have agreed to accelerate research into "smart" airbags that could detect when children are in seats.

No dollar figure or timetable for the research has been set, said Amy Leszczynski, a spokeswoman for the United States Council for Automotive Research. USCAR was formed in 1992 by General Motors Corp., Ford Motor Co. and Chrysler Corp.
The research will be coordinated by the Occupant Safety Research Partnership, which is part of USCAR. Funding will come out of partnership's budget.

Although government and industry executives have not yet agreed on what constitutes a "smart" airbag, one proposal is an airbag that can de-activate itself after detecting when a child seat or child less than a certain weight is in the front passenger seat.
Last month, federal safety regulators said they would push for revisions that would allow automakers to reduce the deploying strength of airbags.

The safety devices have been blamed for the deaths of about 30 children, who were riding in the front passenger seat. Safety advocates have said airbags can also be dangerous to adults with small statures.
Auto industry groups have said they support efforts to make airbags safer. But some executives have questioned the timetables proposed by federal regulators.
Robert Lange, GM's director of vehicle development methodology and labs, said last month it would be difficult to develop the "smart" bags in time for 1999 model year vehicles.
